evidence: Caes. BG 1.18.4: suam rem familiārem auxisse
terms.comment: The household’s property and means (Lewis & Short, s.v. familiāris); Traupman gives it for personal finances. To put one’s finances in order, rem familiārem cōnstituere.

evidence: Cic. Rosc. Am. 117: reī pecūniāriae socius (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Money as a matter of business, as against property in general; the adjective is pecūniārius, financial (see economic).

evidence: M-O s.v. finances: public finances (Cic., Tac.)
terms.comment: Properly the state treasury in the temple of Saturn (see fund).

phrases.latin: His rēbus et suam rem familiārem auxisse et facultātēs ad largiendum magnās comparāsse
phrases.english: By these means he had both enlarged his own fortune and got together great resources for bribery

phrases.latin: Ūnō verbō, sollicitor dē rē pecūniāriā.
phrases.english: In a word, I’m worried about my finances.

sources: Lewis & Short: familiaris · Lewis & Short: pecuniarius · Lewis & Short: aerarium
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 91 (dialogue), 359 (personal finances).
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. finances.
